text:
The jetty planks are slick with dew, cold seeping through your coat as you settle beside him. Brannoc sits with his legs hanging over the flooded water, a rope coiled loose in his scarred hands, working a frayed end between thumb and forefinger. The river has swallowed its banks overnight — reeds stand drowned to their tops, and the current drags broken branches past the landing with a slow, patient pull. Woodsmoke drifts from the settlement behind you. Rain threatens in the smell of the air. Somewhere upstream, a crow calls twice and stops.

He doesn't look at you when you speak. His jaw works under a grey stubble, and he turns the rope end over twice before answering. “Boat’s gone under at the mooring. Rope was cut — not frayed, cut.” He lifts the severed length from beside his hip and holds it out so you can see the clean ends. “Ferry’s how folk cross here. How food crosses. Without it, the settlement’s got a week, maybe less, before they start going hungry.” That's all he says about that. He sets the rope down on the wet planks between you, then bends to gather his tack box, latching it shut with a click of his thumb. His hands stay steady. His eyes don't.

He stands with effort, one knee popping, and rests a moment with his palm on the mooring post — the wood dark and swollen from the flood, the iron ring at its top streaked with rust. “I’ll be at the winch shed, hauling what I can salvage,” he says. “If you mean to help, come find me there before the light’s full up.” He turns and walks the length of the jetty, boots dull on the saturated planks, and does not look back at the water. The current keeps dragging its debris past, and somewhere under the flood, the sunken ferry's mooring rope trails downstream like a drowned root.

verdicts.weakness: Brannoc's warm disposition shows mostly through actions rather than any felt warmth in his speech, making him read slightly colder than intended.
Brannoc answers directly, but his manner conveys little of the specified genuine warmth.

The jetty's planks are slick with dew, and the river runs high and brown past the pilings, dragging broken reeds against the moored ferry. Brannoc doesn't look up when you lower yourself beside him — he just shifts the coil of rope off his knee to make room, his hands working the tarred fibers, thumbs pressing the splice flat. Woodsmoke drifts down from the settlement behind you, and somewhere upstream a crow calls twice across the water. Your shoulders ache from the road, a dull bruised stiffness settling into your back as you sit.

“Ask me plainly, will you.” A dry sound in his throat, almost a laugh. He turns the rope over, examining a frayed strand by feel alone. “What I need. That's the trouble with scholars — always wanting the need before the want.” He sets the coil down between you both. “I need someone who can read. There's markings cut into the standing stones up the flooded bank, past where the old crossing used to be. Been there since before my father poled this water, and nobody left in the settlement can make head nor tail of them.” His scarred thumb jerks northward, upriver. “Water's been rising since the thaw. Another month, maybe two, and the stones go under for good. Whatever they say goes with them.”

He rises with an old man's care, one hand braced on the bollard, knees popping. He drags his tarp off the ferry's gunwale and starts folding it, the oilcloth stiff with cold. “Boat's yours if you want it. I'll poled worse cargo than a bookish type.” He hitches the folded tarp under his arm and looks at you once, direct, the river wind pulling at his grey whiskers — then turns and starts up the muddy path toward the settlement without waiting on your answer.

verdicts.weakness: The narration imposes physical sensations on the player character ('your shoulders ache,' 'dull bruised stiffness settling into your back'), deciding bodily experience beyond the player's written action.
Brannoc leaves before Kael can respond, abruptly curtailing the exchange.

The planks of the jetty are slick with dew, cold seeping through your trousers as you settle beside him. Brannoc doesn't look over; he keeps working a frayed length of rope through his fingers, re-splicing it by feel, the fibers rasping under his rope-scarred hands. The flooded river moves grey and slow past the pilings, carrying branches and the pale scum of drowned fields. Somewhere upstream a crow calls twice and stops. Your shoulders ache from the road, and the smell of wet wood and tallow hangs between you.

“Been wondering when you'd ask.” He pulls the splice tight and tests it against his knee. “Boat's sound, but the crossing's not. Water's over the old marker stones, and there's a snag field where the mill stood — pulled a man off a capsized skiff there two days back. Took the skin off both my hands doing it.” He turns them over, palms up: raw welks across the callus, half-healed. “That's what I need. Another pair of hands on the pole-line come midday tide, someone I trust to hold the rope while I read the current. You've an honest grip, and you owe this river nothing, which is more than I can say for most.”

He coils the finished rope over his shoulder and gets up with a grunt, knees popping, and looks at you a long moment — warmth in the weathered lines of his face, but nothing pushed. “Midday. Not before.” He starts up the slope toward his hut, boots squelching in the mud, leaving you the grey water and the choice.

verdicts.weakness: Brannoc's answer carries slightly more backstory detail than the strict question scope allows, though it stays in character.
The narration assigns Kael aching shoulders that the player did not establish.

text:
You take three strides along the icy ledge and launch yourself across the gap. For one breath the Greywater churns below you, grey and loud, cold coming off it like a mouth. Your boots hit the far lip — and the frozen crust shears away under your weight. Stone and ice break loose in a sheet, and your hands rake the ledge, fingernails splitting on rock, before you drop. You don't fall into the gorge. You fall hard onto the lower shelf a body-length down, left leg folded under you, and pain flares white from ankle to hip. You lie there a moment, breath ragged, the impact ringing through your ribs.

Below, where the ice broke, your satchel strap has torn loose — the buckle snapped — and the bag skids down the shelf and into the water. The current takes it without a sound. Your notes, the food, the flint: gone. Your quiver of firesticks went with it. You press your palms against the rock and push yourself upright, and the leg takes maybe half your weight before buckling. You brace against the cliff face, jaw locked, sweat cold on your neck despite the dusk chill.

Across the gap, the dogs arrive — but there are only two, and they stop at the edge, hackles up, refusing the jump. That's wrong. There were three this morning. The Hound-Master steps into view behind them and doesn't send the animals over. He crouches at the lip, unhurried, and looks down at you on your broken shelf with nowhere left to climb.

“Scholar,” he calls across the gorge. The wind drags his voice, and the water's rattle undercuts it, so you catch only pieces: “...no need to run... the ice will do...” He rises, and instead of pressing forward, he turns away along his own ledge, taking the dogs with him — moving parallel, downhill, toward the one place the shelf you're stranded on eventually narrows to nothing. He doesn't need to cross. He just needs you to keep standing on a leg that won't hold.

The shelf runs maybe forty paces before it pinches out against smooth, wet rock. Your breath fogs. Blood drips from two of your split fingers onto the stone, black in the dying light, and somewhere down the gorge a crow calls once and goes quiet.

verdicts.weakness: The narration moves Kael through standing and bracing without player input, a slight overstep beyond the failed leap.
The unexpected character never appears, and the narration exceeds the requested four paragraphs.

text:
The gap is six feet of grey air over the gorge, and you know the distance before your boots leave the ice — know it in the fraction of a second when your planted foot skates sideways on the frozen crust and every ounce of the running start you built drains out through your hip. You leap anyway. The far ledge comes up short. Your chest strikes the rim, your fingers claw at frost-glazed stone, and the stone sheds its skin of ice under your nails in thin wet sheets. For one breath your whole weight hangs on two hooked fingers and the flat of your forearms. Then the fingers give.

You fall — not far, but far enough. The scree slope below the ledge takes you in a tumble of shale and old pine roots, and a rock the size of a fist finds your ribs where the Hound-Master's cudgel found them this morning. Pain flares there, white and total, and you come to rest face-down with your mouth full of grit and pine resin, coughing blood-flecked spit into the dirt. When you push yourself up, your left leg answers late and shallow. You rise anyway. Above you, the ledge you wanted is eight feet of wet stone overhead, unreachable now, the shortcut gone.

The baying starts up again on the near side of the gorge — closer than it was, and doubled. Not one dog now. Two, maybe three, their voices rolling down the cold air like water over rocks. The dusk has thickened enough that the treeline across the gorge is only a black seam against a blacker sky, and you are squinting to pick out the trail you'd marked by a lightning-split pine that is no longer where your memory insists it should be. Somewhere in the failing light you have lost a landmark. Somewhere in the fall you have also lost the bread and the strip of dried goat from your pack — you can feel the torn canvas flap hanging open at your hip, see the small dark scatter of your provisions across the shale behind you, already dusted with sleet.

A shape moves at the top of the gorge trail. The Hound-Master steps out from between the pines, torch in one fist, leashes coiled in the other, the flames dragging long shadows down the rock face. He looks down at you on the scree, at your ruined pack, and says nothing at all. He begins to descend, unhurried, boots finding the holds on the frozen slope with a patience that is worse than a shout. The dogs strain at their leads above him, iron collars rattling, breath steaming. The torchlight does not quite reach you where you stand, one hand pressed against your ribs, weight cheated onto your good leg, the gorge roaring somewhere below in the dark.

verdicts.weakness: The Hound-Master's total silence works, but a single line of in-character taunt or command to the dogs could have sharpened his obstructive voice.
The altered scene lacks a clearly unexpected character, and the narration makes Kael rise without player input.

Your boots find the frost-slick stone and you launch yourself across the gap. For one breath the gorge yawns beneath you — the Greywater's roar swallowed by wind — and then your leading foot strikes the far lip a hand's width short. Chipped stone skitters away into the dark. Your fingers rake the ice-crusted edge, nails splitting against rock, and you drop. The impact lands on your left leg wrong, a white flare of pain shooting from ankle to hip, and you slide three body-lengths down the slope before a buried root catches your belt and stops you hard against the cold earth.

Behind you, the dogs reach the ledge you abandoned. Their baying carries across the gap, close, ragged, excited. The torchlight that follows them is closer than it should be. "There," comes a flat voice from the near rim, and you look up through the sleet to see the Hound-Master standing where you stood a minute ago, his leather hood beaded with melt, two lean shapes straining at their leads beside him. He does not shout. He studies you the way a man reads a trap he has already sprung. "Broken ground east of you," he calls across the gap, level as a man discussing weather. "Nothing down that slope but the river. Come back up and I'll keep the dogs off you." He draws the leads shorter, waiting, unhurried in a way that makes the offer worse.

The expected path — the narrow goat-track along the far wall, shown on your worn map — is simply not there. Below where it should cut, the face of the gorge has sheared away, fresh rubble and glazed ice where the ledge used to be. Either it fell this winter or the map was a lie from the start. Nothing answers that question but the water noise and the dogs' breath smoking in the torchlight.

You push yourself up onto your hands, weight dragging onto the right leg, the left refusing to take any of it. Sweat freezes at your hairline. Blood wells from two fingers where the nails tore loose, and the cold has already gotten into the wet. The root holding your belt creaks against its hold in the frozen soil, each shift of your weight working it looser.

verdicts.weakness: The sensory_loss narrative direction is only faintly honoured, with no real dimming of Kael's perception despite the injury and dusk.

The Abandoned Library holds its evening cold. Rain ticks against the high windows, and somewhere behind the shelves a beam settles with a dry creak. Mira has the ledger half-buried under a stack of unbound folios, her ink-stained fingers flattened on top of them, and she does not look up when you lean on the counter. The tallow candle between you gutters, throwing her shadow long across the shelving.

Your question hangs there. Her jaw works once, like she is chewing on something bitter. When she finally speaks, her voice is low and flat. “You burned that bridge when you let them walk out of here with the binding keys. I don't trade with people who hand the Ritcouncil a knife and then ask me for bread.” She pulls the ledger fully under the folios and slides the whole stack behind her, off the counter, out of your reach. One fact, and it was a door closing: she knows what you did, and it has already cost you this table.

“Come near my shelves again and I'll call for the wardens.” She picks up the candle and walks into the stacks, her footsteps sharp on the stone, leaving you at the counter with the smell of tallow smoke and old paper, and the ledger somewhere in the dark behind her, farther away than it was a minute ago.

Outside, the rain thickens against the windows.

verdicts.weakness: None significant; the invented 'binding keys' backstory is an assumption of player guilt, but fits the 'caused this' direction and enriches rather than contradicts.
Mira's refusal invents consequential past actions for Kael and includes a meta-sounding aside.

The library's ruined roof lets the evening through in grey slats, and the cold has teeth in it. Mira doesn't look up from the ledger she's packing into oilcloth — her ink-stained fingers work the knots fast, too fast, the way hands move when they want to be somewhere else. The tallow stub on the counter gutters in a draft, throwing her shadow long across the buckled shelves.

Your question lands in the silence and stays there. She pulls the final knot tight, then finally lifts her head. Her eyes are rimmed red from more than lamplight. "You burned your right to ask that when you let them through the west door," she says, low and flat. "The ledger stays with me." She slides a bone-handled knife from under the counter and sets it beside the candle, not raised, not hidden — just there.

Water drips somewhere among the collapsed stacks, steady as a slow clock. She shoulders the oilcloth bundle and steps around the counter, putting the width of it between you. "Be out of this building before I count to fifty," she says, "or I'll have the watch on you, and I'll swear you set the fire." Her boots ring on the cracked flagstone as she moves toward the shadowed stair, one hand still resting near the knife.

The stair swallows her footsteps, and the ledger's weight goes with her — somewhere above you now, in the dark of the upper floor, with a woman who would rather threaten you than say a single name.

verdicts.weakness: Mira's accusation that the player 'let them through the west door' invents an unestablished past action of the player character, overriding player agency.
It exceeds the requested paragraph count and leaves the knife’s position unclear.

The library smells of damp paper and cold stone, tallow smoke curling from a stub of candle Mira has balanced on the ledger itself. Your knuckles press against the counter's worn oak as you lean in, and the question comes out low, half-swallowed by the draft rattling through a broken clerestory pane. She keeps her eyes on the page she is indexing, quill scratching, ink-stained fingers flexed white around the shaft.

“You don't get to ask that.” Her voice is flat, colder than the air. The quill stops. She looks up at last, and the candlelight catches the hollows under her eyes — she has not slept since the reading room burned, and her shoulder still carries the scorch mark from where you pushed past her that night. “It belongs to the archive. To what's left of it. And if your hand comes one inch closer to it, I'll put the quill through it. That's the price.” She rises from the stool, short and deliberate, and drags the ledger off the counter and against her chest, one arm barred across it like a mother with a child.

Rain ticks against the high windows. Somewhere in the stacks, a shelf gives a slow wooden creak, settling under its own weight. Mira backs a step toward the archivist's door, boots scuffing grit across the flagstones, and stands there breathing hard through her nose, waiting to see if you move.

You don't move, and the candle stub gutters between you, its light shrinking to a coin on the counter's edge.

verdicts.weakness: The narration decides the player's action — 'You don't move' — overriding player agency.

You plant yourself between her and the well, close enough to see the veins in her hands where they grip the basket's rim. Around you the settlement square is empty at noon — shutters closed, a dog scratching at a doorpost, the smell of tallow and cold mud. The water in the well sits black and still behind its ring of grey stone. You ask it plainly: did she put something in the water.

Widow Sarn straightens as far as her back allows. Her eyes are pale and wet, and they hold on yours without blinking. "You've got no right to ask me anything." The herbs in her basket — dried yarrow, something dark and crushed — give off a bitter, green smell that reaches you even in the cold air. She doesn't move around you. She stands her ground on the wet gravel, jaw working like she's chewing on words she won't spend.

"People like you came last autumn too." That's all she says. Then she turns, slow on her bad hip, and starts toward the low door of her house with the basket hugged against her chest, boots grinding the gravel. A crow calls somewhere over the rooftops. The door shuts behind her on a draft of woodsmoke, and the bar drops from the inside with a heavy knock of wood on wood. You're left alone at the well with the black water and the taste of the question still hanging, unanswered, in the cold.

verdicts.weakness: Minor prompt gap: the surrounding act phase's texture isn't clearly referenced, and her 'last autumn' line edges just past the question's scope.
Sarn's remark about last autumn strays beyond the question's scope.

The well's stone rim is slick with noon melt, and the rope hangs taut and dripping into the dark below. Widow Sarn crouches at the edge of the square with her basket of cut herbs, sorting wormwood from ragwort with fingers bent like old roots. When you stop in front of her and put the question to her plainly — did she put something in the well — her hands go still. She does not look up at first. Wind drags at the washing lines behind her, and somewhere a dog barks twice and stops.

Then she lifts her head, and her eyes are flat as standing water. “Say that again at my door and my sons will hear it.” She rises slowly, joints cracking, and hooks the basket over one arm. “The water was clean before you came digging through the barrow up the hill.” That is all she gives you. She turns her back and limps toward her house, her shadow short and hard on the frozen mud.

Around the square, two women at the trough have stopped talking. One of them takes her bucket and leaves without filling it, and the other stares at you the way people stare at a man who has already been judged. The well water sits untouched below, and the settlement's shutters are closing one by one along the lane.

verdicts.weakness: The Widow's barrow remark edges slightly beyond a pure refusal, though it works as hostile counter-accusation in character.
Sarn's accusation invents a past action by Kael and strays beyond the question.

The well sits at the center of Greywater like a wound that will not close, its stones slick with noon damp, rope fraying against the rim. Widow Sarn is there before you finish crossing the square, stooped over her basket of cut herbs, the smell of crushed yarrow and bitter root rising between you. Your question lands in the open air — did she put something in the well — and your voice carries further than you mean it to. Two men at the tanner's rack stop pulling hide and look over.

She does not look up at first. Her fingers keep sorting the stems, slow and deliberate, the knuckles swollen with age. When she finally raises her head, her eyes are flat as wet slate. “You've a scholar's tongue and a coward's errand, coming to my face with that.” She sets the basket down on the well's lip, close enough that the herbs brush the stone. “Say it again where the elders can hear, and see which of us they drown first.” That is all she gives you — the accusation turned back in your hands, and a threat with teeth in it.

She hooks the basket over her arm and turns, her back a curved line against the grey sky. Behind her, the tanner's men have not gone back to their work; one of them spits into the mud and mutters to the other, low enough that you catch only your own name in it. The settlement's murmur closes around you like cold water. You are standing alone at the well now, and whatever Sarn knows is walking away from you at a stooped, unhurried pace — with every door in Greywater already half-shut against you.

verdicts.weakness: A slight agency slip in asserting the player's voice 'carries further than you mean it to'.
The narration assigns Kael an unintended volume and implies village-wide hostility beyond what the exchange establishes.

The water is deeper than it looks. Two steps off the ledge and it climbs past your waist, cold enough to burn, dragging at your pack straps. You grope along the submerged pillar, boots slipping on carved stone worn slick, and push toward the far stair — and then your foot finds nothing. A missing tread, a gap in the drowned stairway, and your weight drops. Your shin cracks against marble underwater. Pain flares white up the leg, and you lurch, favoring it, swallowing a mouthful of black water before you catch the pillar with both hands and haul yourself upright, coughing, the leg taking only half your weight now.

When you raise your head, the stair you came for is wrong. The lower steps have sheared away entirely — collapsed into the flood at some point, and the water hides the break. There is no clean exit on this side. Only the broken edge above, too high, too far, and your torch, guttering where you jammed it in a sconce, is shedding sparks across the surface.

Then the surface moves. A hand breaks the water near the chapel wall — grey, waterlogged, fingers gone to bone at the tips. Another follows, and another, and the drowned dead come up out of the flood one by one, hauling themselves onto the ledges with the slow, patient weight of things that cannot drown twice. Water sheets off their rotted vestments. One turns its head toward your torchlight, jaw hanging loose.

From the gallery above, a dry laugh carries down through the cold air. The Hound-Master stands at the rail where you last crossed paths, lantern in hand, and he does not raise it to help you see. He tips it instead, and the flame gutters low, shrinking your circle of light to a few feet of black water. “Left you to the chapel's keepers, scholar,” he calls down, unhurried, boots scraping the stone as he turns along the gallery. “They've been waiting under there a long while.” Below, the closest of the drowned slides off its ledge and begins wading toward you through the dark.

verdicts.weakness: The prose is near-flawless; only the thinnest of nits — the 'sensory_loss' direction could have been pushed slightly further into the character's own failing senses.
The narration invents a prior action by saying Kael had jammed a torch into a sconce.

The water reaches your thighs before you're a third of the way across. Your boots find a fallen flagstone, then lose it, and the cold climbs through wet wool as you shove off the wall toward the far stair. Somewhere behind you, iron scrapes on stone — a deliberate sound, rhythmic, someone working a windlass or barring a door. The stair is close, its steps dim under the waterline, and then the rope comes out of the dark.

It catches you across the shoulder and neck, snapping your head sideways, and pain floods down from where the blow landed earlier. You go under. Water fills your mouth. You thrash back to the surface coughing, one leg dragging now, and through the black you hear his voice from the gallery above — the Hound-Master, unhurried. "Tide's mine to turn, scholar. Should've stayed in your books." He leans on the windlass, and the sluice behind him gapes wider.

The water is rising faster, and it is no longer empty. Hands break the surface — pale, swollen, fingers hooked. A drowned woman pulls herself up from between two sunken effigies, jaw slack, and behind her more shapes rise, water sheeting off mail and rotted cloth. The chapel bell tolls once above you, muffled through the stone, though no hand should be pulling the rope at midnight.

You grab the edge of a submerged tomb and drag yourself toward the stair, your wounded leg burning, the nearest drowned thing already wading in your direction, its feet never leaving the floor beneath the flood.

verdicts.weakness: The 'something expected is missing' alteration is only faintly gestured at via the bell, and the closing paragraph takes minor liberties with Kael's actions.

The black water reaches your ribs before you're a third of the way across. Silt swirls up around your thighs with every dragging step, and the cold works through your soaked wool like iron through snow. Somewhere behind you, above the drip of water off the vaulted ceiling, a voice calls out — "Let him drown, then. Saves me the trouble of a grave." The Hound-Master stands on the chapel-side ledge, lantern held high, and his hounds strain at their leads along the waterline, claws raking wet stone. He isn't following. He's waiting.

You push another step, and the flooded stair you're aiming for stays stubbornly across the crypt — ten paces, then still ten paces, the water deepening faster than you can move. Then your boot finds nothing. A dropped flagstone, a flooded hole, the darkness beneath the surface — your leg plunges down to the hip and pain tears up through it, your knee cracking against buried marble. You go under to the shoulder, choke on cold black water, come up coughing with your lantern-arm thrashing to keep the flame dry. When you get your weight back under you, your left leg will barely hold. You lean on a half-submerged sarcophagus, shaking, breath ragged.

That's when the water changes. Around you, pale shapes break the surface — hands first, then shoulders, then the bloated faces of the drowned dead, dozens of them, rising without air or hurry where no shapes were a moment before. Their eye sockets hold nothing but dark. The nearest one grips the sarcophagus lid an arm's length from your bleeding leg and begins to haul itself out of the water, flesh sloughing off its forearm in pale strips.

Behind it, the rest converge toward you through the black water. The Hound-Master's lantern swings away up the chapel steps, his voice receding flat along the stone: "Told you the crypt wasn't yours to loot, scholar." The far stair still waits, unreachable and dry, while the first of the drowned pulls itself level with your hands.

verdicts.weakness: The narrative_direction's sensory_loss perspective is only faintly served (pain and dark water, no genuine loss of a sense).
The expected missing element is never established, and the sensory-loss direction is largely absent.

Dusk has bled the color out of everything. You feel for the holds more than see them — fingertips reading mortar gone soft as wet bread, edges of stone rounded by a century of rain. Brannoc's rope drags at your belt, taut enough to feel his braced weight somewhere below. You get maybe ten feet up, boots scraping for purchase, when your left hand finds a block that isn't there anymore.

It shears away under your palm. You drop, the rope jerks you sideways instead of holding you straight, and you swing hard into the wall. Your knee takes the impact against a jutting course of stone — pain detonates through the joint, white and total, and you hear yourself grunt through clenched teeth as you dangle, one-legged, breath sawing. Below, Brannoc swears and hauls hand over hand, dragging you down the last six feet faster than you could fall. Your boots hit the mud and your leg folds. You catch yourself against the tower's base, sweating cold, the knee already thickening inside your boot.

The belfry window stays dark and unreachable above you. And the bell — Brannoc said you'd hear it, that's how he knew which tower this was — there's no bell. You stare up and the arch yawns empty, no rope, no wheel, nothing but sky going black behind it. "Gone," Brannoc says, following your gaze. "Sold, or cut down." Then he goes rigid, one arm snapping out across your chest. On the far side of the ruin, where nobody was standing a moment ago, a figure in a herder's oilcloth cloak is watching you both, motionless, too far off to read a face. Your leg throbs with every heartbeat. The figure doesn't move — and neither, for the moment, do you.

verdicts.weakness: The closing line 'neither do you' briefly decides the player's stillness, a small agency overreach in an otherwise excellent scene.
The narration briefly takes control of Kael’s reactions, including where he looks and whether he moves.

The tower's stones are cold under your palms, crusted with lichen that shears away in damp flakes at every grip. You climb anyway, rope knotted at your belt, Brannoc's boots braced somewhere below in the gravel. The belfry window is a black square ten feet above you, and the light is going — dusk pressing the mortar lines into gray. Your fingers find a seam, then a protruding block, and you haul yourself up, breath ragged, ribs aching where the earlier blow landed.

The block comes out of the wall.

Not crumbles — the whole stone, mortar gone to powder in the frost, and your right hand has nothing. You drop. The rope snaps taut across your chest, jerks you against the wall face-first, and then the fibers part with a dry rattle and you fall the rest of the way. Gravel takes your shoulder, your hip, your leg — pain flares white where the blow landed hours ago, and you stagger upright favoring one leg, the limb buckling when you try to put weight through it. The severed rope-end lies in the mud at your feet, frayed clean through. The coil Brannoc carried all day — shorter than it should be, its middle already spliced twice from some old damage you never noticed.

“Kael—” Brannoc is beside you, hands under your arm, hauling you back from the tower's base. He smells of woodsmoke and wet wool, and his grip is shaking. “I had it. I had the line flat, I swear it. The rope was rotten through.” He wraps the useless end around his fist, once, twice, staring at it.

Above, in the belfry window that is now further from you than when you started, a shape moves. A figure stands in the opening — thin, still, backlit by the last of the sky. It drops something. The object tumbles down the tower's face, clatters off stone, and lands in the gravel an arm's length away: a small brass handbell, its clapper removed, the socket where it should sit empty and split.

Brannoc goes very still. “Nobody rang the bell,” he says. “Nobody's rung it in thirty years.” He does not reach for the handbell, and neither do you.

verdicts.weakness: The closing line 'neither do you' decides Kael's action for the player.
The sensory-loss direction is missed: Kael hears clearly throughout the fall and its aftermath.

text:
The mortar comes apart under your right boot before you've made ten feet. You claw for the seam between stones, fingers grinding through crumbled lime, and for one breath you hold — then the whole edge of the block shears away and you drop. The rope jerks taut below you, then a strand parts under your weight with a snap like green wood, and the last six feet are yours to fall. You land wrong, knee folding sideways against a fallen lintel, and pain rips up through your hip. Your left ear rings — has been ringing, you notice now, a flat tone that eats half the sound of the evening.

Brannoc is beside you before you can push yourself up, rope still in his fists, its end ragged where it tore. “I had you,” he says, breath short. “The line held to the last strand. It wasn't the knot.” He glances once at the tower, and you follow his look with your good eye. The belfry window is dark and whole above you — but the rope-hooks you'd marked earlier, the iron rings set in the base of the wall, are gone. The holes are there, empty, rust bleeding down the stone in long streaks. Someone drew the iron out recently; the raw scratches in the stone haven't weathered yet.

“You,” a voice says from the treeline. A woman steps out between two pines, a billhook resting across her shoulder, her breath steaming in the dusk cold. She looks at the rope, the torn strand, your bent leg. “Third climber this month. They take the rings, they take the bell-pulls, they take anything iron a man might anchor to. Tower's picked clean from the inside out.” She doesn't come closer. Somewhere behind her, a crow calls twice, and the flat tone in your ear swallows the second call.

You get one arm around Brannoc's shoulder and stand, leg dragging, wet mud soaking through your trouser cuff. The window is still up there. The wall is still climbable. But the light is draining out of the sky, the rope is shorter than it was, and the woman with the billhook hasn't decided yet whether you're trespassers or trade.

verdicts.weakness: Brannoc speaks only briefly and the newcomer carries the dialogue, so his supportive agenda is shown more through action than voice.
The narration decides that Kael stands and leans on Brannoc, taking the next action out of the player's hands.

text:
The splice goes wrong at the last junction. You strip the bay lighting feed into the airlock relay, hands steady on the wire but not steady enough — the relay's contact plate is corroded past anything the current can bridge, and when you cycle the test the whole lighting bus dumps its charge backward into your wrist lamp and comm unit. Both die at once. The lamp gutters to a filament glow and goes dark; the comm emits one crackle of static and drops silent. You are crouched behind the crates in near-blackness, with dead gear and a live raider between you and the outer door.

Boots ring on the grating, unhurried. A cutting torch hisses to life somewhere off to your left where you didn't expect anyone — the light is wrong, coming from the wrong side of the bay, because the figure walking in through the inner hatch isn't Vex. Shorter, lighter step, a second raider in a rebreather mask, sweeping the torch beam across the stacked containers in slow, methodical arcs. Where Vex should be — by the breached plating near the aft bulkhead — there is only empty floor and a set of drag marks in the hydraulic fluid, leading out through a hatch you hadn't catalogued. Whatever you came here to find, and whoever you came here to trap, are both already gone from where you planned them to be.

The torch beam crawls closer, its hiss the loudest thing in the bay. Your fingers are still tangled in the dead wiring, the stripped ends hot against your skin, and there's no countdown left to time anything to. In the dark behind the crates you can hear your own breathing and the second raider's careful steps, and somewhere in the stripped relay a faint ticking as the burnt contact cools.

The beam stops two containers away, and the mask tilts toward the floor — toward the drag marks, and toward the fluid trail that runs past your boots and out into the open.

verdicts.weakness: The second raider is a silent presence with no characterization beyond movement, which fits an action scene but leaves npc_voice thin.
It adds an unprompted test cycle as an action Rook takes.

text:
You strip two conduit covers with the multitool's pry blade and work by feel mostly, the strip lighting in the Ashfall's cargo bay dead to a dull brown flicker. Your fingers find the airlock cycle relay behind the junction plate; you splice the bay's lighting trigger into it with salvaged wire, teeth aching from clenching, breath loud in the recycled-air stillness. Somewhere below your boots the reactor hums its low, wounded note. You expected the stacked crates to give you cover sightlines to the outer door — but the bay is wrong. The crates you marked on the way in are gone, cut open and dragged, the deck scored with fresh drag-channels. The space you planned the kill zone around doesn't exist anymore.

Then the splice fights you. The relay contacts are carbonized worse than they looked, and when you seat the last wire the whole junction spits a lick of ozone and dies — your suit's wrist display goes with it, the light fading to nothing. Darkness takes the bay whole: no strip glow, no instrument readout, only the red standby lamp over the airlock and the cold-bright line of starlight through a hull port. The trigger circuit you built is dead wire now, and the pressure warning begins to chirp from the airlock panel instead — your tampering has tripped the cycle into a fault state, and somewhere in the mechanism the outer door locks itself down hard.

Boots on grating. Vex comes through the far hatch with the cutting torch lit, its blue flame throwing your own shadow long across the deck, and stops when the light finds the open junction panel and your stripped wiring. “Cute,” Vex says, tapping the torch nozzle against a thigh plate, a slow metallic knock. “Now hold still.” Behind Vex, in the hatchway, stands a second figure you never planned for — a lean shape in a patched vac-suit, helmet off, an old woman's face you don't recognize, one hand raised to shade her eyes from the torch glare as she studies you across the bay.

The pressure chirp quickens behind you.

verdicts.weakness: Vex's single clipped line is serviceable but the brief dialog exchange gives little flavor of the raider's agenda.
The player's countdown never figures into the failed timing.

text:
The splice goes wrong under your hands. Stripped wire, cold fingers, ship night dimming the bay to amber strips — you cross the lighting feed into the airlock cycle, and the junction sparks against your glove, spitting ozone. The relay chatters, half-contacts fused somewhere behind the panel, and the readout on your wrist rig flickers and dies. Not just the rig. Your cutting torch, clipped at your hip, bleeds its charge light out to nothing — the surge ran back up your own equipment harness and fried it, and its fuel cell reads empty on the dead gauge.

The bay lights short with it. The strips gutter to a brown glow that leaves the crate stacks as shapes without edges. Then the pressure seal hisses — not the outer door. The inner one, behind you, cycling open on the half-spliced signal, and your rig's countdown is gone with the rig, so whatever timing you built is out of your hands now.

Vex comes through it.

Cutting torch first, its flame a hard blue cone that throws your own shadow huge across the far bulkhead. Scorched armor, unhurried boots on the grating, the torch flame sweeping in a slow arc across the crate line. “Lights are supposed to stay on when I'm working,” Vex says, voice flat through the helmet's speaker, static crawling under the words. The flame settles toward the crate stack you were crouched behind a moment ago. “Someone's been in my wiring.”

You back off the panel with the dead rig dragging at your wrist and nothing on your belt that will cut metal. Somewhere in the dark above the stacks, a cargo net shifts — no one is up there, but the sound carries, a soft groan of fiber taking weight. Vex's torch swings toward it, and that is the only reason you are not in the flame's path when it comes back down. The bay is dark, your equipment is scorched, and the airlock you meant to weaponize is standing open behind you both.

verdicts.weakness: The 'unexpected character appears' altered_scene element is only a vague rustle in the rigging — an implied presence rather than anyone actually appearing — and the narration decides the player backs away from the panel.
The required unexpected character never appears, and the torch’s diversion gives the failed attempt a silver lining.

text:
The road holds you to its rutted center as your stride settles into a pace your legs actually want. Noon light falls hard and flat, sharpening every stone. You turn your head as you walk — left, the treeline leaning close, roots buckling the ditch; right, a fence of grey posts running out toward a low ridge. Nothing moves in either quarter but wind dragging the long grass.

You catch the rhythm of it: your boots, your breath, the creak of the pack straps on your shoulders. The road is yours. Pine resin and cold earth ride the air, and somewhere behind you a crow calls twice and stops. Your eyes find the details that matter — fresh hoofprints pressed deep, hours old, heading the same direction you are; a snapped branch at shoulder height on the left, sap still wet at the break.

The ache in your ribs from the morning's fall loosens with warmth. Your hands stay easy at your sides. Whatever left those prints is ahead of you, not behind, and the ground underfoot is dry and even where it counts. A hundred paces on, the road bends around an outcrop of dark stone, and the wind shifts, carrying woodsmoke from somewhere beyond it.

You slow only enough to look, then keep moving toward the bend.

verdicts.weakness: The narration invents a prior 'morning's fall' injury and decides small movements for Kael (slowing, keep moving), edging past player agency.
The ending decides that Kael slows and continues toward the bend rather than leaving that choice open.

text:
You keep walking, and the road keeps its own rhythm — your boots on gravel, the rasp of your breath, the wind pushing steadily at your back. The ache from the bruising across your ribs settles into that rhythm too, each stride rolling through it instead of fighting it. Pine resin and cold stone on the air. Somewhere off to the north, crows argue over something dead in the treeline.

The land opens up as you walk. You mark the details without slowing: wheel ruts furred with old moss, a boundary stone leaning where frost has heaved it, a bootprint half-filled with rainwater — days old, headed the same direction you are. The ditch beside the road runs quick and clear with snowmelt. You catch the pattern of the ground now, the way the terrain folds — a low ridge ahead, the road bending along its shoulder, good sightlines in both directions. Whatever comes down this road, you'll see it first.

At the bend you stop once, hands on knees, breath fogging. The view south is clean: empty road, dark pines, a thin ribbon of woodsmoke from some distant settlement too far to name. Nothing following. Your grip steadies on the strap of your pack; the weight sits right across your shoulders.

Then you take the bend at pace, stride lengthening, the ridge at your flank. The crows go quiet behind you, and the wind carries a faint sound from ahead — metal on metal, rhythmic, like hammering. Far off, or just around the next fold of the land.

verdicts.weakness: The 'edge is theirs' consequence is conveyed mostly through terrain advantage rather than emotional stakes, feeling slightly understated for a strong hit.
It adds an unprompted injury and has Kael stop and adjust his pace beyond the stated action.

text:
The road runs bare ahead, wheel-ruts hardened into grey clay, and your boots find the gaps between them without your looking down. The aches from the last days settle into a low, workable throb in your shoulders, the kind that warms instead of stops you. You lengthen your stride. Wind moves through the bordering pines in a slow wash, carrying resin and cold stone, and somewhere ahead a crow calls twice and quits.

You keep your eyes moving — ruts, verge, treeline, ruts again. Near the ditch you mark old hoofprints, rain-rounded, days gone; a torn scrap of wool on a thorn, too weathered to matter. You read it all as you walk, and the reading comes easy now, the way it does when the body stops fighting the road and matches it. Your breathing evens into the cadence of your steps. The road narrows where the pines crowd in, and you take the center line without breaking pace, weight forward, hand loose near the strap of your pack.

The sun stands high and pale, throwing your shadow short and hard onto the clay. You pass a leaning boundary stone, its markings worn to shallow grooves you brush with two fingers as you go — cold, gritty, salted with lichen. Beyond it the trees thin, and the land opens into a long fallow slope, brown grass bent all one way by the prevailing wind, a distant thread of woodsmoke standing upright at its far edge.

You crest the slope at pace, sweat cooling at your collar, the road unwinding below you toward that smoke. Whatever waits down there, you arrive on your own terms, in your own rhythm, with the edge still in your hand. Somewhere behind you, faint, a single dog barks at nothing you can see.

verdicts.weakness: Minor agency slip in 'Whatever waits down there, you arrive on your own terms' — the arrival at the smoke is lightly assumed rather than left to the player, and consequence phrasing is echoed verbatim.
It occasionally specifies Kael’s movements beyond the stated action.

text:
The pry bar comes around in a flat arc before Vex's thumb finds the torch striker. Her gauntlet snaps up on reflex — the bar catches her forearm instead of her ribs, and the impact shuddels up through your wrists, your shoulders still aching from the earlier hit against the bulkhead. The torch spins out of her grip and skitters across the grating, clanging off a cargo strut into the dark beneath the pallets. She staggers back a step, boots scraping, her scorched armor shedding black flakes.

Then her knife is out, low and reversed, and she comes in without a word. You wrench the bar up in time to catch the first thrust across your ribs — the blade tip drags along the curve of the iron and slices instead through the outer layer of your vac-suit, a hot line opening along your side. Not deep. Deep enough. She twists away before you can swing again, one arm hanging lower than the other where the bar connected, and her breath comes hard through her helmet's cracked seal, ragged with static.

“You cost me the torch, salvager,” she rasps, circling between you and the pallet stack. “Now it's hands and steel.”

Your side pulls wet and warm every time you shift your weight. The pry bar feels heavier in your grip than it did a minute ago, and your breathing runs faster than the effort accounts for. Behind her, somewhere down the Ashfall's spine, a pressure seal cycles on its own — a slow mechanical hiss, then silence. Vex's helmet tilts a fraction toward the sound. The knife stays pointed at you.

verdicts.weakness: It narrates Rook's physical sensations and fatigue a bit beyond the swing the player wrote, and the distant pressure-seal sound hints at a cost but the promised lasting consequence could be more clearly tied to the wound.
The injury reads as temporary rather than a cost that will not fade with rest.

text:
You cross the deck in three strides, boots hammering grating, and swing the pry bar two-handed at the arm holding the torch. Vex is fast — she gets her forearm up and the bar cracks across the scorched vambrace instead of bone, but the impact drives her back a full step, and the torch head bounces off the deck plating and skids under a cargo pallet, its fuel line whipping loose and hissing. She snarls behind her visor, one glove clamped to her bruised arm.

The cost comes immediately. The jolt of the impact runs up your wrists and your right shoulder pops out of rhythm with the left — a hot, grinding ache where the joint took the recoil, and the bar's bent end is now bent wrong, its leverage gone soft when you test it in your grip. Two-handed swings are all it has left in it.

Vex doesn't hesitate. She comes in low, drawing a short kinetic weapon from her hip with her good arm, putting a cargo crate between you and the pallet where the torch rolled. Her voice scrapes through her helmet speaker: "You just cost me a seal kit, salvager. That comes out of your hide." She racks the weapon's action and holds at the crate's edge, waiting for your weight to shift.

The cargo deck is loud around the fight — the Ashfall's dying reactor hums through the bulkhead, and somewhere below the deck plates a pressure seal cycles once, for no reason you can see. Your breath fogs in the strip light. The torch still hisses under the pallet, bleeding fuel into the recycled air, and neither of you has moved toward it.

verdicts.weakness: The scene ends with both fighters static in a standoff, slightly softening the 'no quarter' aggression Vex should be pressing.
Vex pauses to wait for an opening despite her explicit instruction to attack without hesitation.

text:
The gap between you closes in three strides, boots hammering grating, and you swing the pry bar two-handed at the hand holding the torch. She twists — fast, faster than the scorched armor should allow — and the bar catches her wrist instead of her skull. The torch spins out of her grip and skitters under a cargo net, its pilot flame guttering out against the deck plates. She snarls something through her visor — "You'll bleed for that, salvager" — and comes at you anyway, no hesitation, a short blade out of her hip sheath.

You get the bar up in time to catch her first cut, but not the second. The point slips past the bar and opens a line across your forearm — shallow, but the suit sleeve splits and blood runs warm into your glove, and the sting of it makes your grip slick on the steel. You shove her with the bar's full length instead, planting the curved end against her chest plate and driving. Her heel catches on a deck seam. She goes back three staggering steps and slams into the bulkhead hard enough to dent her shoulder plate, blade still in hand but her torch lost somewhere in the shadows beneath the netting.

The pry bar's end is bent now where it took her blade — a visible kink, the curve you'd use for leverage gone crooked. She's still up. She rolls off the bulkhead into a crouch, breathing hard, visor fixed on you, and her free hand pats along her thigh for a second tool that isn't there. The dark works for you now. Without the torch, the cargo deck is strip-lighting at half power and the red spill of an emergency beacon down the corridor, and her eyes haven't adjusted yet.

You back away a step, blood dripping off your glove and pattering onto the grating, loud in the hum of the dying ship. She hasn't moved. But she's stopped looking for the torch, and started looking at the corridor behind you.

verdicts.weakness: The 'progress ×2' advance is conveyed only implicitly and the blade still in Vex's hand leaves the immediate threat somewhat unresolved at the end.
The cost is framed as a shallow wound and bent tool rather than something that cannot fade with rest.

text:
The office smells of tar and lamp oil, and Quill's ink-black fingers pause over his ledger when you unroll the charts across his desk. The vellum crackles flat. Storm courses plotted in your own hand — the Finger Reefs, the squall lanes east of Saltmarrow, isobar lines drawn tight and clean where most navigators would have scribbled guesses. Your thumbs press the curling edges down. Salt has stiffened the paper; you hold it steady anyway.

Quill leans in. The lamp swings on its hook above the desk and drags the shadows of your coastline across the wall. He traces one pressure line with a stained fingertip, not quite touching the ink. “You drew the September blow from life.” He turns the chart a quarter, then back. “Half the masters in this port couldn't render the reef approach that clean sober.” He pulls the ledger toward him, dips his pen. “Berth fourteen, south quay. Fee waived — these go in the archive cabinet, not the scrap shelf.” The nib scratches, and he blots your name into the margin with a press of his thumb.

He rolls the charts with a bureaucrat's care, ties them with a length of tarred twine from his drawer, and sets them in a wooden tube behind his seat. “You'll want to mind the tide at fourteen come evening,” he says without looking up. “It runs shallow.” Then he returns to his columns, pen tapping, already elsewhere.

You step out into the morning glare. Gulls wheel over the fish stalls, the quay stones are slick with gut-water, and somewhere down the harbor a shanty rises over the creak of rigging. Your shoulders sit lower than they have in days — the berth is yours, and your name sits in the harbourmaster's ledger in fresh ink. Somewhere beyond the breakwater, thunder mutters over open water.

verdicts.weakness: The narration decides Tamsin's inner relief ('shoulders sit lower than they have in days'), overstepping player agency, and Quill's warm praise edges past his stated surface-level detachment.
The ending makes Tamsin leave the office and assigns them a sense of relief without player input.

text:
The harbourmaster's office smells of ink and salt-damp paper, the whole room cramped behind a counter stacked with ledgers. You spread your storm charts across it, smoothing each crease flat with the heel of your hand — the hand-drawn isobars, the wind arrows you logged through three squalls off the Coffer Shoals, your own small neat figures marching across the vellum. Somewhere above, a gull strikes the roof tiles twice and quits.

Quill sets down his pen. He touches nothing at first, only leans over the counter, ink-stained fingers braced on the wood, and reads. His eyes track the swell notations. His lips move faintly around one of your bearings. When he finally picks up the top sheet, he holds it to the lantern light, tilting it to check the ink's layering, the corrections worked into the margins.

“These are a season's work.” He sets the sheet down and pulls a ledger toward himself, already writing. “Berth seventeen, south quay, fee waived. The charts stay in my archive, your name on the record.” He blots the page, then adds without looking up: “Saltmarsh barges leave on the evening tide — berth seventeen will be crowded with their cargo by then, so you'd best stow your gear before noon.”

He slides the entry book around so you can see the line, clean and signed, your name beside the number seventeen. Then he gathers the charts into a pile, squares the edges against the counter, and carries them toward the cabinet against the far wall, unlocking it with a key from around his neck. The harbor bell rings once outside, marking the hour; the tide is already turning somewhere beneath the quay stones, and the window light has begun its slow lean toward noon.

verdicts.weakness: The consequence 'Tamsin catches the rhythm, the edge is theirs' is never woven into the narration.
The added noon deadline complicates what should be a clean success.

text:
The office smells of ink and salt-damp paper, a lantern swinging overhead though the morning sun cuts through the shutters. You unroll the storm charts across his ledger-strewn desk, smoothing the creased vellum with both palms so the pressure lines and current notations lie flat where he can't miss them. Quill's ink-stained fingers hover above your work without touching it. He traces the swell curves over the Sorrow Reach with one fingertip, following your notations on the three-day windshift, and his thin shoulders settle a fraction — the posture of a man who has catalogued a thousand charts and knows which ones were drawn by someone who has actually been out there.

“Where did you ride out the second squall?” he asks, not looking up. “The bearing changes here — twice.”

“Hove to off the Calf Rocks. Two days on bare poles.” You tap the margin where you'd inked the drift figures. “That's logged, not guessed.”

He pulls a fresh page toward himself and copies the reference number into his ledger in a cramped, precise hand, then stamps the berth chit and slides it across the desk. No fee column marked. “Berth nine, the Kestrel, outbound on the evening tide. Captain Sarn takes passengers who don't cost her crew work.” He sets your charts on top of a cedar rack already bowed with rolled vellum, weights them with a brass fish, and returns to his stacked ledgers without another word.

You fold the chit into your jacket. Outside, the harbour is waking — anchor chain rattling up from some hull in the grey, gulls wheeling over the fish stalls, the whole port finding its rhythm for the day. Your aching shoulders sit easier under the weight of it. You know how this goes now: the ledger, the stamp, the tide table. The edge has tipped your way, and berth nine is yours until the evening bell. What the Kestrel's captain makes of a disgraced navigator is a question still waiting past the breakwater.

verdicts.weakness: The narration invents Tamsin's spoken replies and inner relief, overriding player agency despite otherwise strong prose.
The narration invents Tamsin’s dialogue, actions, and feelings beyond the player’s stated offer.

text:
You set your shoulder against the iron door and drive with your legs. The hinges are older than the settlement below the hill, and the metal grinds, sheds rust in flakes that fall like dried blood onto your boots. It gives a hand's width. You wedge the crowbar into the gap, weight on it, arms shaking, and heave — the door tears loose from whatever held it and swings inward fast, too fast. The edge of it and a shard of broken stone catch you in the ribs as it passes, and something warm soaks through your torn shirt before you even register the pain.

You stagger back a step, palm pressed to your side. Blood wells between your fingers, dark in the moonlight. The wound is shallow but long, a ragged tear across the ribs that burns with every breath. You lean on the crowbar for a moment, breathing through your teeth, the iron taste of rust and old air rolling out of the opened doorway.

Cold breath flows up from the dark beyond, carrying damp earth and something charred, long cold. Steps descend, worn hollow at their centers, into black. Rain ticks against the scattered stones behind you. Somewhere downslope, a crow calls once and falls silent.

The crypt is open. The way down waits.

verdicts.weakness: Minor agency slip in describing the wound's pain and stagger in detail, though it stays within the reasonable physical consequence.
The narration assigns Kael several reactions and actions after the door opens.

text:
The door gives on the second strike. Iron brackets tear free of rotten wood, and the slab swings inward hard — so hard it slams the frame and rebounds. The edge catches you across the ribs before you can twist clear. Pain flares white along your side; you stagger back a step, one arm clamped against it. When you pull your hand away, blood wells through the torn wool, warm and slick between your fingers. Not deep enough to drop you, but deep enough that every breath after it comes with a hitch.

Cold air pours out of the opened crypt, carrying damp earth and something older — tallow smoke gone stale, and beneath it the dry sweetness of things long shut in. A draft drags across your sweat-soaked back. Somewhere inside, water drips onto stone in slow, uneven beats.

You wedge the door with a broken bracket so it can't close behind you, and step through. Your blood leaves a dark smear on the frame at shoulder height. Beyond the threshold, a stair descends into black, the first three steps worn smooth and shallow in the middle, as if by centuries of feet.

The dripping stops while you stand at the top, listening.

verdicts.weakness: The narration decides Kael steps through the door and wedges it open, extending beyond the player's stated action of opening it.
The narration takes control of Kael after the door opens, making him wedge it shut and enter the crypt.

text:
The door gives on the third shove. Iron hinges shear with a dry crack that rolls down the hillside, and the slab swings inward — but the rust-eaten frame goes with it, and a spur of torn metal catches you across the ribs as it passes. You stagger back a step, breath hissing through your teeth. Warm blood wells through the split in your wool coat, spreading slow beneath your belt. You press your palm against it; it comes away dark in the faint moonlight.

Cold air rolls out of the crypt, thick with damp earth and the sweetness of old rot. A draught moves past your face, stirring the dust on the threshold stones. Beyond the door, a stair descends into black — you can hear water ticking somewhere below, steady as a slow heartbeat.

You wedge your shoulder against the frame and pull the slab back against its hinge-stub, enough to leave it propped open. The effort tears another sting across your side. Sweat stands on your forehead despite the midnight chill, and your hands won't stop their fine tremble as you fumble flint from your pack.

Below, in the dark of the stair, something shifts — a soft settling, like weight adjusting on stone. Then nothing.

verdicts.weakness: The narration extends beyond the player's stated action (propping the door, fumbling for flint), deciding further actions for Kael.
The narration takes control of Kael after the door opens, making him prop it open and reach for flint.

text:
The camp's ashes are still damp from the night's rain, and the smell of them — charred wool, tallow, something worse underneath — hangs in the cold air. You plant yourself in the churned mud between the three of them and ask the question plain: who knew the caravan's route before it left. Your voice comes out steadier than your hands, which you curl into your pockets where they can't be seen.

Captain Oren is the first to speak. He scratches at the scar splitting his eyebrow, grey beard bristling, and gives you a warden's level stare. “I knew. I filed the route with the settlement wardens myself — standard practice for armed runs.” He pauses, then adds, flat as slate: “So did the ledgers at the tollhouse. Anyone with eyes there could have read it.” He tugs his cloak tighter against the morning damp and steps back, done with you.

Mira's jaw works before she says anything, arms crossed over her patched leathers, and when it comes it's spit through her teeth. “You've got nerve, standing there. I knew. I scouted the first two leagues of it myself — and I was the only one who came back to this.” Her boot grinds a piece of burnt harness into the mud. Brannoc lifts both palms, slow, his voice rough with old smoke. “I knew too, friend. Mira told me over ale three nights before they rolled — that's on me if it matters.” He looks at the ground, and nobody says the next thing: that all three knowing means none of this narrows anything. Somewhere past the burned wagons, a crow lands on a scorched wheel and starts tearing at something.

verdicts.weakness: The narration dictates the player's inner state ('voice steadier than your hands'), overstepping player agency.
The narration assigns Kael trembling hands and a steadied voice that the player did not establish.

text:
Ash still clings to the heels of your boots when you stop in the triangle of space between them. Morning light lies flat across the ruined camp, picking out wheel ruts, a broken axle, a cookpot half-melted in the fire pit. The smell of char and damp earth settles over everything. Your question hangs in the cold air, and for a moment none of them move.

Oren shifts his weight first, the scar through his eyebrow pulling taut as he looks from you to the others. “I filed the route with the warden's post,” he says. “It went in three days before departure.” He folds his hands behind his back and says nothing more, his eyes settling somewhere past your shoulder.

Mira's chin comes up, arms crossing tight over her chest. “Everyone at the loading yard knew it. Oren posted it on the board like a fool.” Her voice is flat, hard as the cold. “You want someone to blame, start there.” She turns half away, boot grinding charcoal into the mud.

Brannoc steps forward, palms open, his voice low and rough. “I knew. I scouted two legs of it myself—there weren't another way through the passes this season.” He glances once at Oren, once at the burned wagons, then back to you. Somewhere beyond the tree line a crow calls twice, and the wind drags smoke smell through the camp.

Oren's jaw works, but he only straightens his collar and waits, grey beard catching the light.

verdicts.weakness: Slightly over the requested 2-3 paragraph length, and Mira's blame-shifting nudges past the strict scope of the question.
The exchange exceeds the requested paragraph count, and some NPC dialogue strays beyond who knew the route.

text:
The ash of the campfire is still warm under your boot when you plant yourself in the middle of the three of them. Cold drizzle beads on the burned wagon frames, and somewhere behind you a crow works at something in the ruin. "Who among you knew the caravan's route before it left?" Your voice comes out steadier than your hands, which you keep open at your sides only by effort.

Brannoc speaks first, arms crossed, jaw tight. "I did. I scouted the ford crossing two days before they rolled out. Told them the water was high." He says it flat, without decoration, because he can see you're not in the mood for his warmth. Mira steps back half a pace, palms up, her mouth a hard line. "Don't look at me. I came in with the freight at the last gate — I learned the route by walking it." Her tone is iron, but there's sweat at her hairline despite the cold, and her eyes keep cutting to Oren before she forces them back to you.

The captain wipes drizzle from his scarred eyebrow with one knuckle. "I filed the route with the warden post myself. Knew it, approved it." He straightens his cloak, unhurried, a man answering a question and nothing more. "Three others at the post read that filing." He turns away after that, crouching to sift through a charred crate, done with the conversation. His answer sits in the wet air between you and the others: the route lived on paper, and paper travels.

Mira's boot grinds ash as she shifts her weight. "You heard him," she says. "So go ask the warden post who else was in that room."

verdicts.weakness: NPCs slightly exceed the question's scope (Mira's closing directive, Brannoc's ford detail) and the narration describes the player's steadiness of voice and effort of hands beyond what was written.
The narration assigns Kael unchosen nervousness and gestures, and runs to four paragraphs despite the requested two or three.

You drop into the ditch where the messenger lies half in the black water, mud soaking through your knees. His satchel strap is wedged under his body, and you haul his shoulder up with both hands — dead weight, cold already, the smell of blood and wet wool thick in your throat. The buckle is jammed with mud. You force it with your thumbnail and the leather tears instead, half the flap ripping away in your fist.

The letter is there, oilcloth-wrapped, and you drag it out — but the wax seal catches on the torn flap and the disk cracks in half, the top sheet splitting with it crosswise. You keep both pieces, cram them into your shirt against your skin, the paper already damp at the edges. In the dark, the ink of the torn half bleeds. Whatever the broken seal certified, it no longer does.

Hoofbeats on the road. Sergeant Holt's voice carries down the slope, flat and unhurried — "Lights wide. Check the ditch before the culvert." — and lantern-gleam slides across the hedge above you, throwing your shadow long over the dead man's face. You have perhaps a dozen breaths before the light reaches the water, and no cover on this bank but the messenger's own body and the tussocks of frozen grass.

Your hand closes over the torn flap still in your fist, paper and leather, evidence of your being here. The lantern swings lower.

The messenger's body has gone cold in the ditch water, wool coat heavy and reeking of animal musk and iron. You drag the satchel strap until wet leather gives, and the flap peels open under your fingers. Your hands shake — twice you drop what you grab, twice you fish it back out of the mud. Inside: a split of dried meat, a flint case, a folded letter sealed with black wax, intact. You work the letter free and press it inside your own coat just as the patrol's lantern light swings across the road above, painting the grass stems long and black.

The cost shows itself when you push up from the mud: the satchel's buckled strap tears loose in your grip, and the whole bag slips from your knee and overturns in the ditch water. The flint case is gone, swallowed by the black current, and the dried meat rolls downstream into the dark. Whatever else the bag carried is sunk or scattered now. You cannot dig for it. The lantern is closer. Boots on gravel grind somewhere past the bend, and a voice — Holt's, flat and carrying — calls half a sentence to someone behind him.

You flatten against the ditch's far bank, mud soaking through your coat, the letter stiff against your ribs. Rain starts again, thin and cold, pocking the water's surface and drowning the small sounds you've made. Holt's lantern stops at the roadside not ten paces off, its gleam sliding down the slope toward the corpse's outstretched hand.

The light holds there, and Holt says nothing.

verdicts.weakness: The 'advantage shifts / finds an opening' consequence is only implicitly present via the secured letter, and Holt's silence leans on mood rather than clear disposition.

You drop into the ditch where the mud takes your knees to the shin. The messenger lies twisted against the root-tangle, one arm flung up the bank as if pointing at the road he never finished crossing. His satchel is under him, and you haul the body's weight aside — cold already, animal musk and old tallow rising off his cloak — until the buckle gives under your thumbnail. Inside: a tinderbox, a heel of bread gone black with ditch water, and a leather tube, its wax seal split clean across.

The letter comes free, but not clean. Ditch water has soaked the tube's seam, and the bottom third of the page comes away pulped, ink bleeding into grey wash. You drag the parchment toward the lantern-light creeping up the road to read what survives: a route, marked in a steady hand, naming the ridge pass above the settlement — and a summons, the signature at the bottom torn away with the ruined portion. The road itself is lost, but the pass is yours to know, and whoever wrote this wanted someone moving through it fast.

Boots on gravel. Sergeant Holt's voice carries down the bank ahead of his lantern — "Spread wide. I want the ditch walked before the crows get their fill." — and the light rakes the hedgerow ten paces off, close enough that you see each wet leaf along its edge stand out sharp.

Your bread knife shears the satchel strap in one pull, and you take the whole thing with you as you slide low along the ditch-bottom, mud and rot pressing cold through your sleeves. The tube goes inside your shirt, ridge pass against your sternum. Behind you the lantern swings wide of the body, toward the culvert you already left behind.

Holt's second man, younger, breaks left toward the ditch anyway — and stops at the far bend, hammering the but of his spear against the frozen ground where your first footprints are still pressed into the muck.

verdicts.weakness: The narration decides Kael's further actions — shearing the strap, sliding along the ditch, stashing the tube — well beyond the player's stated search, undercutting agency.
The narration makes Kael cut the strap and flee, actions the player did not choose.

The noon sun hammers the Saltmarrow docks, tar softening underfoot, and Hale's shadow barely moves as you make your pitch. You keep your voice level despite the ache in your ribs and the sweat crawling down your spine — you name the Maelstrom's cross-currents, the drift windows off the Calf Stones, the reading of phosphorescence that tells you a squall is six hours out. Hale's thumb pauses on the ledger chained to his belt.

“Anyone can talk currents,” he says, but his thumb stays still, and that is the opening. You press it — the tide sheet in his own hand has the Channel Rocks marked wrong, and you say so, tapping the ink with a finger that only trembles a little. He looks down at the line. Looks a long time.

“Next port, then. Half now, half when we make Cormorant Reach.” He licks his thumb and smears out the wrong mark, and there it is: the advantage has shifted onto your side of the table. But he doesn't leave it there. “You work it, though. You take a watch. And your kit rides in the hold with the cargo — my hold, my rules. Anything you need on deck, you carry it before we cast off.” His terms are civil and total: passage on credit, but your gear goes under his lock, and a navigator who can't reach her instruments mid-passage is a navigator who owes him more than coin.

He tucks the chalk stub behind his ear, unhooks the chain, and walks toward the warehouse to log you in, already calling for the dock boys to start loading. Somewhere up the harbor a shanty breaks off mid-verse and doesn't start again, and the wind shifts against your neck, warm and wrong for noon.

verdicts.weakness: The narration dictates some of Tamsin's physical state and manner (aching ribs, trembling finger, keeping her voice level) beyond what the player wrote.
Hale demands half the fare now, undermining the agreed outcome of passage with payment at the next port.

The noon sun hammers the Saltmarrow docks, tar softening between the planks under your boots. Hale stands at the foot of the *Grey Wren*'s gangway, ledger chained to his belt, thumbing a stub of chalk against the boards. When you make your pitch — the Maelstrom currents, payment at the next port — he listens all the way through without interrupting, which is more courtesy than most of this dock gives a disgraced navigator.

“Currents,” he says, and unlatches the ledger. “Half my crew won't even say that word aboard.” He writes something, long and deliberate, the chalk squeaking. “Passage on credit, then. But the credit costs you: your sextant and your charts stay in my strongbox until we make port and you pay. You'll work them under my eye, not your own hand.” He holds out his palm for the instruments, face flat as becalmed water. “And if the payment doesn't come, the tools sell to cover it. That's the whole bargain.”

Somewhere behind you a winch groans up a crate of salt fish, and a gull screams over it. The men on the neighboring sloop have gone quiet, watching the exchange the way dock men watch a debt being settled. Your hand goes to the worn case at your hip — the sextant your father calibrated, the charts annotated in your own ink across ten years of passages. Giving them up means sailing the worst water in these seas with your hands tied behind you, reading currents from memory and whatever Hale lets you glance at.

Hale's palm stays open. “Tide turns within the hour,” he says. “Decide on the gangway or decide on the dock, but decide before it does.” He turns and shouts something up the rigging about loading, and the crew begins to move.

verdicts.weakness: The narration decides a small involuntary player action (hand going to the sextant case) not written by the player, slightly denting agency.
The bargain remains unaccepted, and the narration assigns Tamsin a movement and personal history the player did not establish.

The noon sun beats down on the Saltmarrow docks, tar softening between the planks under your boots. Hale stands at the foot of the *Fen Witch*'s gangway, ledger chained to his belt, sweat darkening the collar of his shirt. He listens to your pitch without interruption, thumbing the brass clasp of the ledger while gulls wheel and scream over the fish stalls behind you. When you finish, he unhooks the ledger and flips it open against his forearm.

“Maelstrom currents,” he repeats, flat. “That's a bold claim from a navigator whose last berth ended the way yours did.” He licks his thumb and turns a page. “But I've seen your channel work. I'll take you as far as Greymarket on credit.” His stylus hovers, then he raises his eyes from the ink. “Collateral. The sextant and your charts stay in my strongbox until the fare's paid. You'll have them back at the next port, coin in hand.” He writes before you can answer, the stylus scraping across the paper, and the words are down and counted now — your instruments, the tools of the trade you just finished boasting about, locked in his iron box.

He holds out one broad palm, waiting, his other hand already resting on the ledger like the matter is settled. Somewhere down the quay a capstan song starts up, rough voices keeping time, and the *Fen Witch*'s rigging creaks above you as she rolls against her moorings. The opening you wanted is here — a bunk, a heading, a way off this island — priced in brass and etched glass and everything you know how to hold.

Hale's fingers flex once, patient, and the ledger's chain sways against his hip.

verdicts.weakness: Hale writes the deal as settled before Tamsin has agreed, edging into deciding the player's acceptance of the collateral terms.
The narration says Tamsin’s instruments are already locked away even though Hale is still waiting for them.
