The ledger is there under Mira's palm, but when your fingers close on the leather spine, her other hand comes down across your knuckles like a dropped bar of iron. You pull — the book doesn't move — and then she's up off her stool faster than a woman her size should be, and the stool's leg catches you across the knee. Pain flares white up your thigh. You stagger back into a shelf, and dry rot and loose pamphlets rain down over your shoulders, old paper catching in your collar, dust coating your tongue so thick you cough and can't hear what she says next. The world is grit and ringing.

“You were watching my hands,” Mira says, low, while she draws the ledger off the counter and threads her arm through it like a farmer carrying a chicken. “The whole time at the door. Watching, waiting for me to look away.” She circles the counter's end, putting the wide table between you, and her boots are deliberate on the warped boards. There is a poker beside the cold hearth and she takes it up — not brandishing it, just holding it, the way a woman holds a tool she's used before.

You get your weight off the shelf. Your knee takes the load badly; something in it grinds and you have to plant your palm flat on the wood to stay upright. When your eyes clear the tears the dust wrung from them, you see the far corner of the room — and it is wrong. The iron sconce that hung there is gone. Bare chain swings against the wall in the draft, and the hook's screw-holes are raw, fresh shavings of pale wood still clinging below them. Someone took it tonight, while you and Mira were circling each other at the entrance.

Then the door behind you bangs wide and cold evening air drives in across the floor with the smell of pine resin and wet iron. A man fills the frame — broad, muffled to the chin in sodden wool, a pack-frame taller than his head. He looks at you, at Mira, at the ledger under her arm, and takes his time about all three. “Mira,” he says. “This one yours?” She doesn't answer. She backs another step, poker low, ledger tight against her ribs, and the swinging chain behind her keeps turning in the draft.

verdicts.weakness: None significant; the narration weaves every prompt element seamlessly into a tense, sensory-rich failure.
The stranger’s arrival adds tension, but the required fateful escalation remains unclear.

The ledger is not under her hand. Your fingers find only damp pulp where the pages should be — someone has torn the whole block out, leaving a stub of binding and a scatter of browned fragments across the counter. The spine sits there gutted, and Mira's hand is already moving.

She catches you across the temple with the iron edging of a lamp stand, a short brutal arc you never see coming. White fills your vision. Your knees hit the floorboards and the room tilts, one ear full of a high thin ringing that swallows every other sound — her voice becomes shape and breath without words. The right side of your face burns where the blow landed, and when you push yourself up on one arm, your leg buckles under you and you go down again against the counter's base, tasting copper.

Through the ringing and the swimming dark, a second figure moves in the doorway behind her. A man, broad through the shoulders, travel-stained wool, a forester's axe resting loose in one hand. He watches you on the floor without hurry, without surprise, the way a man watches something he was told to expect. Mira straightens her sleeve and steps between you and the counter, keeping what remains of the ledger at her back.

You get one boot flat under yourself and stop there, breathing against the ache, blood threading from your hairline into your brow. The ring in your ear thins enough to let one sound through — the man's voice, low and unhurried, saying something to Mira you cannot yet make out. Neither of them looks away from you.

verdicts.weakness: Mira and the forester remain silent, defensible under sensory loss but leaving their agendas slightly under-voiced.
The narration dictates Kael’s attempts to rise after the blow.

The ledger is not where you remember it. Mira's hand rests flat on empty wood — the book is gone from the counter entirely, and the absence stops you mid-step behind it, half-crouched, boot scraping damp flagstone. That scrape is what gives you away.

She turns faster than an old woman should. The iron poker is already in her fist — it must have been leaning against the counter's inside face, hidden all evening — and she swings it low and mean, not at your head but at your thigh. It lands with a dull, heavy crack through wet wool. Pain flares white down the leg and your knee buckles; you stagger into a shelf and old books cascade around your boots, spines splitting, paper smell and dust thick enough to taste. Your ears ring with the blow, and for a moment the room narrows to sound only — her breathing, your own, the rattle of a loosened shelf board somewhere above.

“Thieves come in pairs,” Mira says, not raising her voice. She plants herself between you and the doorway, poker low, and behind her, in the doorway itself, a man is standing where no one was standing a breath ago. Broad shoulders, travel-stained cloak still beaded with rain, a scar running through one eyebrow. He looks at you, then at her, and says nothing. He blocks the light from the corridor the way a wall blocks a draft.

Your leg will not hold your full weight; when you try to shift, the knee folds and you catch the shelf again, breathing hard through your teeth. The ledger is nowhere in reach, and Mira's eyes have gone flat and cold, whatever curiosity she had at the entrance burned clean away.

verdicts.weakness: Mira's cryptic single line is effective but brief; a touch more of her voice would strengthen the confrontation.
It briefly dictates Kael’s next movement rather than leaving that choice to the player.

You sprint. The crates pass in a blur of scuffed composite and stenciled warnings, your boots hammering the grating, and Vex's torch beam sweeps past your shoulder and misses — it bites into the crate behind you instead, spitting a spray of molten slag across the deck plating. The heat washes against your neck. You keep moving.

You vault a snapped cargo strap, palm stinging where you catch the edge of a crate, and the control panel is there — recessed into the bulkhead, screen glowing faint amber under a skin of dust. You slap your hand on the interlock and the panel wakes under your fingers. Somewhere above, hydraulics groan, and the mag-clamps on the outer bay doors cycle to standby with a heavy clunk that rolls through the deck.

“Back off,” you say, or maybe you don't — your throat is dry and your pulse is loud in your ears, and the words come out rough either way.

Vex rounds the crates at a run, torch up, but the geometry has turned. You're at the panel now, and the panel is the edge of everything on this deck: atmosphere dumps, clamp releases, the doors themselves. Vex's boots stop hard on the grating ten meters out. The torch's pilot flame hisses in the recycled air. Behind the scorched visor, breath comes fast and ragged.

“You press that, we both die in vacuum,” Vex says. One gloved finger taps against the torch's fuel valve — a slow, deliberate tick of metal on metal. “Mather's paying me double to bring you in breathing. Don't test my arithmetic.”

Then Vex steps back behind the crate stack, torch still raised, boots grinding grit into the grating. The panel glows under your hand, and your own breathing is the loudest thing in the bay.

verdicts.weakness: The narration puts dialogue in Rook's mouth ('Back off'), deciding the player character's words despite the hedging.
It puts unchosen words in Rook’s mouth and exceeds the requested paragraph count.

You sprint, boots hammering the grating, and Vex's torch swings after you. The flame kisses the edge of a crate as you vault past it and sparks spray across the deck, scorching your sleeve but finding nothing else to burn. You skid around a stack of hull plate, feel the heat wash over the metal an arm's length behind you, and keep moving. The recycled air tastes of ozone and burnt polymer. Somewhere below, cargo restraints groan against their bolts as the derelict's frame shifts.

Vex misjudges the spacing. The torch's hose snags on a tie-down cleat and the flame sputters, dragging the raider half a step off line — just enough. You dive the last three meters, palms slapping the cargo control housing, and haul yourself upright against the console. Your shoulder screams where you clipped a stanchion on the way in; you ignore it and slap the guard cover up. Strip lighting flickers overhead, half the panel dead, the rest glowing a sick instrument-green.

“Stop —” Vex's voice cracks through the torch mask, ragged with effort. The raider rounds the crates at a run, but you're already at the panel, fingers flying over the keypad. “That hold's mine. I bled for it.”

You key the lockdown. Magnetic seals thump home along the hold's spine, one after another, a falling rhythm you can feel through the deck plates. The bay door between Vex and the controls begins to cycle shut, hydraulics hissing, and Vex pounds a gauntleted fist against it once before backing off, torch lowered but still lit, the flame washing the corridor in orange.

“Fine. Keep your scrap, salvager.” Vex retreats a step, cutting the torch down to a pilot flame. “But the Ashfall didn't die on her own. Something ripped bay three open before I ever got here — and you just sealed yourself in with it.” The raider turns and walks back into the dark of the corridor, boots ringing on grating, armor trailing the smell of scorched composite.

You stand at the console, breath sawing, bruised knuckles resting on the keypad. The hold beyond the viewport sits in shadow, and somewhere in it, faint and irregular, cargo shifts against cargo — a sound with no engine behind it.

verdicts.weakness: The minor injuries (scorched sleeve, clipped shoulder) edge slightly toward adding costs to what was ruled a clean success.
The narration turns a clean race to the controls into an injury and an unchosen lockdown that traps Rook with a new threat.

You sprint. The crates pass in a blur of scuffed plasteel, your boots hammering the grating, your breath ragged in the recycled stink of the Ashfall's dead air scrubbers. Vex's torch flares behind you — a hiss of ionized gas and a wash of heat across your shoulder blades — but the cutting stream rakes high, splashing off a container two meters to your left, molten slag spitting across the deck plates. You drop low, slide on hydraulic fluid, and come up running.

Vex works the torch in a rhythm: charge, vent, cut. You catch it on the third pulse — the venting cycle, a half-second where the nozzle goes dark to purge heat. She's venting now. You cover the last stretch in that gap, palms slamming the cargo control housing, fingers finding the recessed panel. The console is cold under your hands, its screen cracked but live, instrument glow bleeding through the fissures. You key the lockout. Somewhere below, mag-clamps engage with a shudder that climbs through the deck and into your knees. The hold's cargo masters answer to you now, not to her torch.

“Cheap move, salvager.” Vex's voice comes flat through her helmet speaker, static crackling under the words. She kills the torch and lets it hang from its tether, one gauntlet flexing. Her scorched armor creaks as she steps around the last crate, unhurried, keeping her sidearm leg in view. “Controls won't feed you if you're dead.”

She's right about that much, and your body knows it — a tremor in your grip you can't fully close down, bruises from the earlier fall aching down your ribs with every breath. But she stops at the edge of the sealed section, torch dead, the hold's lockdown lights striping her armor amber. Whatever she came for is behind your lockout now.

The venting cycle counts down somewhere behind the wall, a slow hiss through the pipes.

verdicts.weakness: The narration assigns Rook involuntary internal states (tremor, awareness 'she's right') that brush past player agency.
It assigns Rook an involuntary tremor and an earlier injury, then runs to five paragraphs despite the four-paragraph limit.

text:
You kneel in the rubble where the watchtower's spiral stair folded in on itself, dragging aside stones slick with rain-moss. Charcoal, old and crumbled — a fire ring near the base, small, built by one person keeping their head down. A tallow stub burned down to a coin of wax. You work deeper, and your fingers find leather: a satchel strap, half-rotted, snapped. Beneath a shifted lintel your knuckles split on a jagged edge of iron; blood threads down your wrist and soaks into the dust, and the strap tears further as you haul it free, whatever it once carried long gone. The leather is stiff with two winters of weather. Whoever camped here is not coming back.

The dark came early inside the stairwell, and it still does. You scrape your palm along the inner wall and the rubble shifts under you — a slab tilts, and daylight drops through a gap where the fallen stone had wedged itself against the outer wall. A triangular opening, wide enough for shoulders, breathing cold air that smells of pine resin and damp earth from the moor beyond. The tower's collapse sealed this side for years; your digging is what opened it.

You crouch at the gap, blood dripping off your fingertips into the mud. Bootprints dimple the soft ground beyond the opening — old, rain-rounded, but paced evenly, someone walking unhurried away to the northeast. Crows argue somewhere over the ridge. The wind pushes through the gap and past your face, cold against the sweat on your neck.

You flex your split hand and watch the dark under the far side of the rubble, where the floor drops away into something the light doesn't reach.

verdicts.weakness: The discovery that the contents of the satchel are 'long gone' slightly over-resolves the player's question about who was here without leaving a hook to pursue.
Rain-softened bootprints beyond an opening sealed for years create a timeline contradiction.

text:
You work the rubble with both hands, dragging aside a slab of frost-split stone until your shoulders burn. Underneath, the old floor survives — charred planking, a hearth swept flat by the collapse. You dig through ash and find what you came for: a boot print pressed into the soot near the fire, adult-sized, heel worn on the outside edge. Beside it, a clay pipe stem snapped clean, still smelling faintly of pine resin tobacco. No green in the moss creeping over the fallen stones. Whoever sheltered here came within the last few days and moved on.

You lever another beam aside to follow the prints, and the rotten wood shears without warning. A splinter as long as your thumb drives through the back of your glove and into the meat of your palm. You hiss through your teeth, pull free, and blood wells hot against the wet leather. The glove is torn — useless against the cold now, and the ache in your hand settles in deep.

But the beam was hiding something. Where it lay against the tower's base, mortar has crumbled away into a gap wide enough to squeeze through — a stairwell mouth descending into the tower's undercroft, breathing out cold air that smells of damp earth and rust. The prints lead straight to it. Whoever they belonged to went down.

Wind drags low across the moor behind you, and somewhere out in the heather a crow calls twice and stops. The gap waits, dark and drafting. Your blood keeps time against the torn leather.

verdicts.weakness: A few second-person actions (hissing, pulling free) edge past strict player agency, though they follow naturally from the injury.
The narration makes Kael hiss and pull free, deciding reactions and actions the player did not specify.

text:
You work through the rubble on your knees, gloves slick with wet grit. The tower fell inward, its stones heaped in a spine of mossy iron and slate, and under the fall of the second-floor beam you find what the rain hasn't taken: a leather satchel split along one seam, a tin cup dented flat, three arrowheads rusted into a single lump. Whoever camped here cut their firewood from the beam itself — old chop-marks, grey and weathered, softened by at least two winters of rain. They left in a hurry, or didn't leave at all. You work the beam aside to get at the space beneath, and the stone it's braced on shifts with a grinding crunch — you wrench your hand back, but not before the edge of your pack catches and tears, and a fistful of dried meat and your spare flint drop through the gap into the dark below, gone somewhere you can't reach.

The gap they fell through is worth the loss. The collapsed beam has levered a floor-slab up on one side, leaving a wedge of black opening down into the tower's undercroft, and cold air pushes up out of it, carrying the smell of damp earth and old tallow. You wedge a loose stone under the slab's edge and press down on the beam until the opening holds wide enough for your shoulders. Soot-blackened rungs are set into the wall just inside — someone used this way before you, climbing down, and the lowest rung you can see gleams faintly with worn iron where hands gripped it.

A crow calls twice from the ridge behind you, and the wind drags a low rattle through the loose slate overhead. Rain is coming; you can taste it in the air, cold and mineral, and the light is already going amber and low across the moor. Whatever is down there has waited this long. Your fingers are numb, your shoulder aches where the beam caught it, and the dark under the slab is breathing cold against your face.

verdicts.weakness: The consequence 'momentum +1 / advantage shifts' is well conveyed, but npc_voice can only be neutral here as no NPCs exist, and the cost (lost supplies) is slightly mild for a weak hit.
The narration decides Kael wedges the slab open and gives him an aching shoulder without player input.

text:
Mira turns toward the broken window at the far wall, one hand lifting the shutter to squint at the grey evening outside, and in that beat her weight shifts off the ledger. You move. Your boots stay on the edges of the boards where the rot hasn't taken hold, and your fingers slide the leather-bound book out from beneath her palm before the pressure of her hand can return. The cover is cold and damp, swollen at one corner, and it fits flat against your ribs as you ease back behind the counter's remains.

She turns back. Her eyes—pale, rimmed red from the smoke that still hangs in the rafters—go straight to the empty space on the counter. "Where is it." Not a question the way most people ask questions. Her knuckles whiten on the shutter's edge. "That's not yours to take, scholar. I told you at the door—this place takes a toll from everyone who walks in."

You keep the table between you, and the ledger stays where you've tucked it. The room holds its chill around you both: water dripping somewhere behind the shelves, the sour smell of wet vellum and ash. Mira steps away from the window, boots deliberate on the boards, but you've already read her rhythm—she guards the counter, not the door. The gap behind the toppled shelf to your left is three strides of open floor, and she knows it too. Her jaw works once, twice, and she reaches instead for the iron poker leaning against the cold hearth.

Somewhere above, in the rafters, a crow shuffles and drops a single downy feather through the smoke-stained air.

verdicts.weakness: The poker-grabbing escalation at the end edges a clean STRONG_HIT toward a fresh complication, softening the clean success the result demanded.
Mira immediately discovers the theft and reaches for a weapon, turning a clean success into a complication.

text:
Mira turns toward the broken window at the far side of the hall, one hand lifting to shade her eyes against the last grey light, and you move. Two steps across the rotted floorboards, boots placed where the wood is thickest, and you crouch behind the counter. Dust coats everything — the ledger lies open beneath her pressed palm, its pages stiff with damp. You slide a folded scrap of parchment from your coat and work it under the book's spine, easing it free an inch at a time. Her fingers rest on the wood now, on nothing.
